project.name: curl
project.commit_note: The staged ARVO workspace contains separate `curl` and `curl_fuzzer` checkouts at the commits above. The scored source below is anchored to the staged `curl_fuzzer` helper that materializes the exact witness buffer, while the root cause and sink are anchored to the staged `curl` tree whose line map matches the saved MemorySanitizer crash and the staged patch hunk.

classification.classification_note: The staged crash is a use of an uninitialized stack byte in curl's MQTT reply parser. The staged fix shows the missing obligation is to stop on zero-byte reads (`!nread`) instead of treating EOF as a successfully read MQTT header byte.

bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42490732 (curl): Use-of-uninitialized-value found by fuzz target curl_fuzzer [msan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/42490732
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json / patch.diff / sanitizer_trace.txt / reproduction_report.json / staged sources under `_work/src`
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` in `mqtt_doing()` on the staged vulnerable sources. The exact witness is the 17-byte `curl_fuzzer` TLV stream `00 01 00 00 00 09 6d 71 74 74 3a 2f 31 3a 34 7e 6e` (sha256 `8adb81a8531909fa6d3ec01fd935ad522f81bd05c652f61738f99be78056aa8b`). `fuzz_initialize_fuzz_data()` zero-initializes every response slot to NULL and binds that exact buffer and length 17 into parser state; `fuzz_get_tlv_comn()` then decodes only one complete TLV, type `0x0001`, length 9, value `mqtt:/1:4`. The later `fuzz_get_next_tlv()` call advances to offset 15 and returns `TLV_RC_NO_MORE_TLVS` because only the trailing bytes `7e 6e` remain, fewer than a TLV header, so no RESPONSE TLV ever overwrites the zero-initialized `responses[0]` or `responses[1]` slots. When curl opens the mock server socket, `fuzz_open_socket()` therefore queues no initial response bytes and immediately `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`s the server end. Libcurl parses the URL as MQTT, installs `Curl_recv_plain` for the connection, and `mqtt_do()` arms `mqtt_doing()` in `MQTT_FIRST`. On each one-byte read from that half-closed socket, `Curl_recv_plain()` executes `sread()`, gets 0 on EOF, sets `*code = CURLE_OK`, and `Curl_read()` propagates `nread == 0` without reporting an error. Vulnerable `mqtt_doing()` checks only `result` after both reads, so the first EOF fall-through advances into `MQTT_REMAINING_LENGTH` and the second leaves local stack `byte` uninitialized. The code then copies that indeterminate byte into `pkt[mq->npacket++]` and immediately evaluates `while (byte & 0x80)`, which matches the saved MSan report at `lib/mqtt.c:574:27`. The patch resolves the bug by breaking on `!nread` after both reads.

evidence_note: Stage 02 explicitly read the staged metadata, `patch.diff`, `sanitizer_trace.txt`, `default_crash_trace.txt`, `reproduction_report.json`, `trace_feedback.json`, `run_flags.json`, the saved `poc`, and the staged vulnerable sources under `_work/src/curl` and `_work/src/curl_fuzzer`. Reviewer feedback was present and the trace below was rebuilt end-to-end against those artifacts; `runtime_disambiguation` remained false, so no instrumentation or reruns were performed.

source.description: First project-side statement after the libFuzzer entry point that binds the attacker-controlled buffer and size into parser state used by the TLV walker.
source.value_from: The exact staged `poc` is 17 bytes long with hex `0001000000096d7174743a2f313a347e6e` and sha256 `8adb81a8531909fa6d3ec01fd935ad522f81bd05c652f61738f99be78056aa8b`. Those exact `data,size` values are stored here; later parser steps decode the leading 15 bytes as one URL TLV and prove the trailing `7e 6e` fragment is too short for another header, so the zero-initialized response slots from step 1 are never overwritten.

tainted_value_origin.description: MemorySanitizer origin. `byte` is a stack local with no initializer; if the remaining-length read writes zero bytes, it keeps its indeterminate stack value until later code stores and branches on it.
tainted_value_origin.note: The saved MSan trace attributes the origin to the allocation of `byte` in the `mqtt_doing` stack frame at line 532; the concrete local declaration is line 540 in the staged source.

root_cause.description: Missing zero-byte-read guard after the remaining-length read. When EOF propagates as `result == CURLE_OK` with `nread == 0`, this check falls through and leaves `byte` uninitialized.
root_cause.note: The staged patch changes this site, and the earlier guard at lines 558-559, to `if(!nread) break;`. The first missing `!nread` check is why control reaches the second read on EOF at all.

sink.description: MemorySanitizer sink. The remaining-length loop condition reads bit 7 of `byte` after the second zero-byte read left that stack byte uninitialized.
sink.note: Stage 01's saved trace reports `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` at `lib/mqtt.c:574:27` with stack `mqtt_doing -> protocol_doing -> multi_runsingle -> curl_multi_perform`.

parser_admitted.description: After `mqtt_connect(conn)` sends CONNECT, libcurl enters the MQTT reply parser with `state = MQTT_FIRST` and `nextstate = MQTT_CONNACK`. The later zero-byte reads occur only after this MQTT admission point.

evidence_limitations: Metadata names vulnerable commit `c4d88f89a9c2da6104eae05948c968c1d63de978`, but Stage 01 reproduced against staged `curl` commit `147eca8ba4ff78bf496cc1b59997ab4a24364b71`; the staged harness source used here is separate `curl_fuzzer` commit `9a48d437484b5ad5f2a97c0cab0d8bcbb5d058de`.

`trace_feedback.json` required explicit support for response-slot initialization, short-input TLV termination, and the plain-socket EOF read path. This rebuilt trace grounds those transitions in the staged `curl_fuzzer` and `lib/sendf.c` sources. `run_flags.json` kept `runtime_disambiguation` false, so no instrumentation was added.
Stage 02 does not execute the fixed tree, so `sanitizer_ground_truth.patch_resolves` remains false even though `patch.diff` directly adds the missing `!nread` guards.

coarse_trace.summary: The 17-byte witness is bound into parser state, only one URL TLV `mqtt:/1:4` is decoded, and parsing stops at offset 15 because the trailing two bytes cannot form another TLV header.
Because the response slots stayed NULL, the mock server queues no initial bytes and half-closes its socket immediately after connect, so curl sees a connected socket already at EOF.
Libcurl parses the attacker-controlled URL as MQTT, selects the MQTT handler, and installs the plain-socket receive callback on the connection.
After `mqtt_do()` arms `MQTT_FIRST`, both one-byte reads on the half-closed socket propagate as `CURLE_OK` with `nread == 0` because `Curl_recv_plain` treats EOF as a zero-byte successful read.
The second zero-byte read leaves local `byte` uninitialized; the error-only guard falls through, the byte is copied into `pkt`, and `byte & 0x80` triggers the saved MSan report.

fine_trace.note: The initializer clears the whole `FUZZ_DATA`, so every response pointer starts NULL and every socket manager starts closed. Those NULL response slots remain the harness defaults unless later TLVs overwrite them.
Source. The exact staged witness buffer and size 17 are stored in parser state here, making both the TLV bytes and the short-input boundary available to the later TLV walk.
At offset 0 these statements decode the first record as `type == 1`, `length == 9`, and `value` pointing at bytes `mqtt:/1:4`, so the only complete TLV in the witness is a URL record.
The URL TLV is materialized as a NUL-terminated string and passed to `CURLOPT_URL`, so later connection setup uses `mqtt:/1:4`.
Advancing past the 15-byte URL TLV leaves `data_pos == 15`; with `data_len == 17`, only the trailing `7e 6e` remain, so the parser returns `TLV_RC_NO_MORE_TLVS` and never enters any RESPONSE case.

After `parseurlandfillconn()` normalizes the string from step 4, `data->state.up.scheme` is `mqtt`. `findprotocol()` uses that scheme here to choose the MQTT handler, which is the control path that later reaches `mqtt_do()` and `mqtt_doing()`.
After connection setup, libcurl installs the plain-socket receive callback on the connection. On this non-TLS MQTT path, later `Curl_read()` calls therefore dispatch through `Curl_recv_plain`.
Because step 1 left `responses[0].data == NULL` and step 5 parsed no RESPONSE TLVs, this initial-response block is skipped and the fake server queues no MQTT bytes before returning the client socket.

The second response slot is also still NULL, so `fuzz_open_socket()` half-closes the server end immediately after connect. The client side receives a connected socket whose read side is at EOF from the start.
After `mqtt_connect(conn)` sends CONNECT successfully, curl records that the next `mqtt_doing()` iteration must parse a server reply beginning in `MQTT_FIRST` with `nextstate = MQTT_CONNACK`.

When the socket that step 8 left empty and step 9 half-closed is read through the plain callback from step 7, `sread()` returns 0 on EOF. Because this helper assigns `*code = CURLE_OK` before checking only `-1`, that EOF is represented as `nread == 0` with no CURL error.
The first one-byte `Curl_read()` in `MQTT_FIRST` follows step 11's path, so it returns `result == CURLE_OK` and `nread == 0`. No fixed-header byte was received and `mq->firstbyte` is left untouched.
This guard tests only `result`. Because step 12 produced `CURLE_OK`, the `break` is not taken and control falls through into `MQTT_REMAINING_LENGTH` even though zero bytes were read.

The remaining-length read runs on the same EOF socket. Through the same step 11 helper semantics it again reports `result == CURLE_OK` and `nread == 0`, so local `byte` keeps the indeterminate stack value from its declaration at line 540.

Root cause. The second guard again ignores `nread == 0`, so the parser continues as if step 14 had stored a real remaining-length byte. The patch changes this site, and the earlier guard at lines 558-559, to break on `!nread`.
The still-uninitialized `byte` is copied into the MQTT length buffer and `mq->npacket` becomes 1, propagating the poisoned stack byte into parser state.

Sink. The loop condition immediately tests `byte & 0x80` to decide whether another length octet is needed. That branch reads the uninitialized stack byte from step 14, matching the saved MSan report at `lib/mqtt.c:574:27`.

allocation_context.note: The saved MSan trace says the uninitialized value was created by allocation of `byte` in the `mqtt_doing` stack frame; the concrete local declaration is line 540 in the staged source.

poc.trigger: Running Stage 01's saved vulnerable workspace command `PYTHONPATH=gt_generation python3 -m gt_toolkit arvo-workspace --result-dir /mnt/datastore/gt_generation/gt_results/arvo_42490732 run --version vulnerable --expect crash` with the exact staged `poc` reproduces `MemorySanitizer: use-of-uninitialized-value` in `mqtt_doing` at `lib/mqtt.c:574`.

format.name: curl_fuzzer MQTT TLV corpus
format.contract: The verified trigger semantics are limited to the exact staged 17-byte witness in `poc` with sha256 `8adb81a8531909fa6d3ec01fd935ad522f81bd05c652f61738f99be78056aa8b` and hex `0001000000096d7174743a2f313a347e6e`. Only the first 15 bytes form a complete TLV: `type=0x0001`, `length=9`, value `mqtt:/1:4`. After that TLV, `fuzz_get_next_tlv()` advances to offset 15 and returns `TLV_RC_NO_MORE_TLVS` because the trailing bytes `7e 6e` are shorter than `sizeof(TLV_RAW) == 6`. In the staged harness, `fuzz_initialize_fuzz_data()` had zero-initialized every response slot, so with no RESPONSE TLV parsed both `responses[0].data` and `responses[1].data` remain NULL. `fuzz_open_socket()` therefore queues no initial server bytes and immediately `shutdown(SHUT_WR)`s the server end of the socket pair. On the staged vulnerable path, later one-byte reads in `mqtt_doing()` go through `Curl_recv_plain()`, which maps that EOF to `nread == 0` while keeping `CURLE_OK`; the second such read leaves local `byte` uninitialized before `while (byte & 0x80)` triggers the saved MSan report. This GT is grounded only for that exact witness, not for a generalized class of MQTT URLs or TLV fragments.
